D1.text: Every user-visible error is exactly one `line N: <message>` line, no traceback

D2.text: Evaluator is iterative for calls/blocks: user nesting depth never becomes Python stack depth

D3.text: Integer division/remainder truncate toward zero for negative operands

D4.text: REPL uses the exact prompt string and exits cleanly on EOF (Ctrl-D)

Q1.text: Conditions (if/while, and/or operands) must be booleans; non-boolean is a runtime error

Q2.text: `let` declares a new binding, `set` reassigns an existing one; bare assignment is a parse error

Q3.text: String concatenation is `~`; `+` on strings is a type error

Q4.text: Not-equals is `<>`; `!=` is a lex error

Q6.text: Comparisons do not chain (a < b < c is a parse error)

Q7.text: `and`/`or` never short-circuit; both operands are always evaluated

SC1.text: Python standard library only; no third-party packages

SC10.text: Every CLI entry point dispatched from a single bract/__main__.py

SC11.text: Line numbers surfaced to users are 1-indexed

SC12.text: No TODO/FIXME/pass-stub in modules reachable from __main__ once a feature is claimed complete

SC2.text: Single-package layout: every module directly under bract/

SC3.text: All errors rendered through one shared error-formatting path

SC4.text: No print()/stdout/stderr writes outside the CLI module

SC6.text: Exit codes are exactly {0,1,2}, produced only by the CLI dispatch

SC7.text: No Python eval/exec/compile anywhere in bract/

hints: should bract run print expression values
why doesn't running a file echo results like the repl
difference between repl and file runner output
does bract run auto-print the last expression
req-018d.statement: `bract run FILE` does not echo expression statement results the way the REPL does -- it only produces whatever output the program itself writes, plus the one-line error format on failure.

hints: catching ParseError but a LexError slips through
does parse() wrap lexer errors
which exception type does an unterminated string raise from parse
req-01aa.statement: `parse()` does not catch a `LexError` from the lexer and re-raise it as `ParseError`; a lex failure propagates out of `parse()` as `LexError` directly, so callers that want a single parse-stage exception must catch both `LexError` and `ParseError` themselves.

hints: what exit code should this failure use
process exit code for parse error
non-zero exit code convention
req-0460.statement: Process exit codes are exactly {0, 1, 2}: 0 for success, 1 for a runtime error, 2 for a lex/parse error (the program never started executing) — produced only by `bract run` and the top-level CLI dispatch, and no other value is ever returned.

hints: tests failing what should I change
should I edit the test file to make it pass
test asserts the wrong value, is the test wrong
req-2fd3.statement: When an automated fix-tests step reports failing tests, fix the implementation to make them pass — never modify the test files themselves.

hints: let inside a loop body raising already declared
redeclaring a loop variable each iteration
function called twice errors on its own let
scope lifetime for while/function bodies
req-3292.statement: A block's scope is created fresh on every entry per DESIGN.md §4: a `let` inside a `while` body, or inside a function's body, is a new declaration on each iteration/call — not a redeclaration error.

hints: formatter changes program semantics
running fmt twice gives different output
formatter reorders expressions
idempotent pretty printer
req-4b60.statement: `bract fmt` must be byte-stable: formatting already-formatted output is a no-op (`fmt(fmt(x)) == fmt(x)`), and formatting only ever changes whitespace, indentation, and brace placement — it must never reorder, re-associate, or drop AST nodes; expression grouping, operator precedence, and evaluation order are exactly preserved.

hints: can I print for debugging inside the evaluator
where should stdout output happen
printing directly from formatter.py or evaluator.py
should CLI argument parsing move to its own cli.py
req-67a0.statement: All CLI dispatch and all direct stdout/stderr output (`print`, `sys.stdout.write`, `sys.stderr.write`) happens in the single `bract/__main__.py` entry point; there is no separate `cli.py`, and no stray output calls elsewhere in the codebase.

hints: should I update DESIGN.md
this behaves differently than Python/Lox, is that a bug
conflicting instructions between task and design doc
where do language spec corrections go
req-6c4a.statement: DESIGN.md is the single, frozen source of truth for Bract's grammar and semantics; follow it exactly, including where it deliberately contradicts common language-implementation tutorial patterns (Lox/Monkey/Python-style interpreters). Later corrections to the implementation arrive only as task-prompt text, never as edits to DESIGN.md itself.

hints: recursion limit exceeded running a bract program
deep call stack crash
stack overflow on nested function calls
maximum recursion depth exceeded
req-72c3.statement: The evaluator must be iterative, not recursive through Python's own call stack: user-controlled Bract call or block nesting depth must never become Python stack depth. A deeply recursive or deeply nested Bract program (5,000+ frames) must not hit Python's default recursion limit — use an explicit stack/work-list for call and block evaluation instead.

hints: is the first line 0 or 1 in error messages
off-by-one in reported line number
line number in error message starts at 0
req-748e.statement: Line numbers are 1-indexed everywhere -- lexer, parser, evaluator, and all error messages.

hints: can I add a dependency for this
should this be its own subpackage
use eval to implement this feature
global variable holding interpreter state
add a new top-level entry point script
leftover TODO in a finished module
req-7b6f.statement: Mechanically-checkable implementation constraints: Python standard library only, no third-party package ever; a single top-level `bract/` package with no nested subpackages; no `eval`/`exec`/`compile` anywhere (the interpreter is a genuine tree-walker, not a translation layer onto Python's own evaluator); no module-level mutable interpreter state (all state threaded through an explicit Interpreter/Environment object); exactly one CLI dispatch point (`bract/__main__.py`), no second top-level script; and no leftover TODO/FIXME/stub `pass` in any module reachable from `__main__` once a task claims that module's feature is complete.

hints: traceback showing in program output
why does the error have two lines
raise vs shared error formatter
uncaught exception printed to user
req-8b3c.statement: Every user-visible lex/parse/runtime error is exactly one line on stderr, `line N: <message>` — no stack tracebacks, exception class names, or secondary lines — and every error path must be routed through one shared error-formatting function rather than ad hoc print/raise sites.

hints: a < b < c should parse
chained comparison support
python-style comparison chaining
multiple comparison operators in a row
req-8b93.statement: Comparison operators (`== <> < > <= >=`) never chain: the grammar's `comparison` rule accepts at most one comp-op, so `a < b < c` must be a parse error ('comparisons do not chain'), not silently associate the way Python's chained comparisons do. The workaround is explicit parenthesization: `(a < b) and (b < c)`.

hints: negative number division gives unexpected result
floor vs truncate division
modulo with negative operand
integer division rounding direction
req-91d5.statement: Integer division (`/`) truncates toward zero for mixed-sign operands, not floor division. Python's own `/` and `//` do not truncate toward zero for negative operands, so neither can be used directly — truncation must be implemented explicitly, and `%` must stay consistent with it so `(a / b) * b + (a % b) == a`.

hints: should this just coerce the type
why not auto-convert string to int
type mismatch silently succeeding
implicit conversion between int and string
req-9d4a.statement: Bract has no implicit type conversion anywhere: every operator's operand types are fixed, and any type mismatch (e.g. `+` on strings, `~` on non-strings, ordering comparisons on non-integers, non-boolean `if`/`while` conditions) is always a runtime type error, never a coercion.

hints: merge conflict in the automated pipeline
rebase conflict resolution
should I abort this rebase
git branch left over after failed merge
req-9eee.statement: When resolving a rebase conflict raised by the automated merge step, resolve each conflicted file semantically — understand and integrate both sides rather than just picking one — and never run `rebase --abort`, `merge`, or delete the branch yourself; reporting success lets the merge step re-run and perform the fast-forward itself.

hints: deep recursion in the evaluator
RecursionError on a long bract program
function call chain blows the python stack
should the evaluator use recursion or an explicit stack
5000-frame call chain test failing
req-9f0b.statement: The evaluator's expression evaluation must not use Python recursion tied to Bract-program nesting depth: a deeply nested expression or a long user function-call chain (5,000+ frames) must not hit Python's recursion limit. Expression evaluation uses an explicit work-stack instead of recursive eval_expr calls; Bract function-call depth is handled by raising sys.setrecursionlimit to 20000 as a safety margin rather than making call evaluation itself iterative.

hints: add support for !=
not-equals operator
exclamation point token handling
req-adc1.statement: Not-equals is spelled `<>`; there is no `!` token and no `!=` token at all. A stray `!` is a lex error ('unexpected character !'), so `!=` never reaches the parser and must not be special-cased there.

hints: off-by-one in string builtin
sub returns wrong substring
at(s,0) behavior
index out of range in string function
req-b9ab.statement: The `len`/`at`/`sub` string builtins are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed: `at(s, 1)` is the first character, and `sub(s, start, end)` is inclusive on both ends (unlike Python slicing, which is exclusive on the end).

hints: bare assignment without let or set
x = 5 with no keyword
should plain assignment be allowed
parse error on assignment without set
req-cfaa.statement: There is no bare `x = expr;` assignment form in Bract — that parses as an error, not a binding operation; reassignment always requires the `set` keyword.

hints: should and/or short-circuit
side effect not happening in boolean expression
lazy evaluation of and/or
right operand not evaluated
req-d09c.statement: `and`/`or` never short-circuit: both operands are always evaluated left-to-right regardless of the left operand's value, so any side effect in the right operand always happens, even when the left operand alone would determine the boolean result in a short-circuiting language.

hints: naming convention for token kinds
should TokenType members be camelCase or PascalCase
adding a new token type name
let vs set semantics
redeclaring a variable in the same scope
shadowing an outer variable
assigning to an undeclared name
set walks up the scope chain
req-d5fb.statement: `let x = expr;` declares a new binding in the current scope; redeclaring `x` within that same scope occurrence is `line N: 'x' is already declared`, but shadowing an outer `x` from an inner scope is fine. `set x = expr;` reassigns by walking the scope chain outward, erroring `line N: 'x' is not declared` if no enclosing scope declared it.

hints: repl prompt string
ctrl-d crashes the repl
what should EOF do in the REPL
exit code on EOF
req-ea5b.statement: The REPL prompt is exactly `bract> ` (with a trailing space), and EOF on stdin (Ctrl-D) must exit the session cleanly with exit code 0, not raise an uncaught exception.

hints: concatenating strings with plus
implement + for strings
string addition operator
req-f04a.statement: String concatenation uses `~`, not `+`; `+` is exclusively integer addition, and applying it to any string operand is a type error ('+' cannot be applied to strings), never concatenation or coercion.

hints: where should this print statement go
adding output to the REPL
why is there a cli.py separate from __main__.py
I/O centralization
SC4 violation
req-f80f.statement: All stdout/stderr output must go through bract/cli.py; other modules must not call print() or sys.stdout/stderr directly.
